\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Home-Based Telerehabilitation After Ischaemic Stroke:\\A Multicentre Randomised Controlled Trial}
\author{T.~A.~Bekele, M.~J.~Laaksonen, R.~Osei, and C.~Vandermeer}
\date{February 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
Exercise-based rehabilitation after ischaemic stroke improves
functional recovery and reduces long-term disability, yet access to
supervised programmes remains limited by geography, transport, and
workforce shortages. Traditional centre-based programmes require
patients to attend supervised sessions two or three times per week, a
demand that many patients discharged to rural areas cannot meet.
Home-based telerehabilitation, in which exercise sessions are delivered
by video link with remote supervision, has emerged as a plausible
alternative that could widen access without diluting the therapeutic
dose.

The evidence base, however, has important gaps. Most telerehabilitation
trials after stroke have been single-centre feasibility studies with
fewer than one hundred participants, follow-up limited to the end of
the training programme, and surrogate endpoints such as balance scores
rather than clinical events. Whether remotely supervised exercise
affects recurrent vascular events, and whether the intervention remains
safe when delivered at scale across centres with differing platforms
and staffing, are the questions that matter for guideline committees.

The present trial was designed to answer these questions. We randomised
patients entering rehabilitation after ischaemic stroke to either
home-based telerehabilitation or usual care, stratified by centre and
by baseline functional status, and followed them for clinical events
beyond the end of the structured programme. The primary hypothesis was
that telerehabilitation would reduce the composite of recurrent stroke,
cardiovascular death, and hospitalisation for any vascular event
compared with usual care.

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Design and Participants}
The trial was conducted at seven rehabilitation centres across two
countries between March 2022 and June 2025. Adults aged 40 to 80 years
were eligible if they had experienced an ischaemic stroke within the
preceding six weeks, were medically stable at enrolment, and had
sufficient cognitive function to follow video instructions. Key
exclusion criteria were severe aphasia, unstable cardiac disease,
inability to perform a baseline walking test, and participation in
another interventional trial. All participants provided written
informed consent, and the protocol was approved by the ethics committee
at each centre.

Randomisation was performed centrally in permuted blocks of variable
size, stratified by centre and by baseline Barthel index above or below
60. Allocation was concealed from the recruiting clinicians until after
enrolment. Because of the nature of the intervention, participants and
therapists could not be blinded, but all outcome events were
adjudicated by an independent committee blinded to treatment
assignment.

\subsection{Interventions}
Participants in the telerehabilitation group received a tablet computer
and attended video-supervised exercise sessions five times per week for
twelve weeks, combining aerobic, strength, and balance components, with
intensity titrated weekly against recorded heart-rate data. The control
group received usual care, consisting of a discharge exercise booklet
and a single outpatient review at week six. Both groups received
identical counselling on diet, smoking cessation, and medication
adherence, and concomitant therapy followed contemporary guidelines.

\subsection{Outcomes}
The primary endpoint was the composite of recurrent stroke,
cardiovascular death, and hospitalisation for any vascular event.
Secondary endpoints included the Barthel index, six-minute walk
distance, health-related quality of life, and each component of the
primary composite. Serious adverse events were defined as events that
were fatal, life-threatening, or required hospitalisation, and were
reviewed by an independent safety board every three months.

\subsection{Statistical Analysis}
The trial was powered to detect a 28\% relative reduction in the
primary composite with 80\% power at a two-sided significance level of
5\%, assuming a control-group event rate of 16\% and allowing for 10\%
loss to follow-up. Time-to-event outcomes were analysed with Cox
proportional hazards models stratified by centre, and continuous
outcomes with linear mixed models adjusted for the baseline value. All
analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle, and missing outcome
data were handled by multiple imputation.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Participant Flow and Baseline Characteristics}
Between March 2022 and January 2025, 1,024 patients were assessed for
eligibility across the seven centres. Of these, 196 were ineligible,
most commonly because of severe aphasia or inability to perform the
baseline walking test, and 84 declined to participate. The remaining
744 patients were randomised, 372 to telerehabilitation and 372 to
usual care. Baseline characteristics were well balanced between the
groups: the mean age was 63.2 years, 31\% were women, the median time
from stroke to randomisation was 4.6 weeks, and 22\% had a Barthel
index below 60.

Adherence to the supervised phase was high in the telerehabilitation
group, with a median of 54 of 60 scheduled sessions completed. At the
six-month contact, 71\% of participants in both groups reported
exercising at least three times per week.

\subsection{Functional Outcomes}
The Barthel index improved more in the telerehabilitation group than in
the control group, with a between-group difference of 4.8 points in
favour of telerehabilitation at the end of the supervised phase, and
the six-minute walk distance differed by 32 metres. Quality-of-life
scores did not differ between the groups at any time point.

\subsection{Clinical Events}
The median follow-up was 12 months from randomisation. A primary
composite endpoint event occurred in 58 of 372 patients in the
telerehabilitation group and in 74 of 372 patients in the control
group. The hazard ratio for the primary composite was 0.76 with a 95\%
confidence interval of 0.54 to 1.08, corresponding to a relative
reduction of 21\% after adjustment for the stratification factors; the
nominal p-value was 0.19. The components of the composite showed
consistent directions: recurrent stroke occurred in 30 versus 41
patients, vascular hospitalisation in 19 versus 22, and cardiovascular
death in 9 versus 11 patients. Table~\ref{tab:events} summarises the
clinical events.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Clinical events during follow-up, by treatment group.}
\label{tab:events}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Endpoint & Telerehabilitation ($n=372$) & Control ($n=372$) \\
\midrule
Primary composite & 58 & 74 \\
Recurrent stroke & 30 & 41 \\
Vascular hospitalisation & 19 & 22 \\
Cardiovascular death & 9 & 11 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Safety}
Serious adverse events occurred in 11 of 372 participants in the
telerehabilitation group (3.0\%) and in 17 of 372 participants in the
control group (4.6\%). No serious adverse event was judged by the
blinded safety board to be definitely related to the intervention. Two
events in the telerehabilitation group, one episode of chest pain
during a session and one fall resulting in wrist fracture, were judged
possibly related; both patients recovered fully. Non-serious falls
during exercise were more frequent with telerehabilitation, affecting
9\% of participants versus 6\% in the control group, and led to
temporary modification of the exercise prescription in most cases.

\subsection{Subgroup and Sensitivity Analyses}
The effect on the primary composite was consistent across prespecified
subgroups defined by age, sex, baseline Barthel index, and centre
volume, with no significant interaction. Sensitivity analyses
restricted to the per-protocol population produced estimates compatible
with the primary analysis.

\section{Discussion}
In this multicentre trial, home-based telerehabilitation produced a
relative reduction of about a fifth in the composite of recurrent
stroke, cardiovascular death, and vascular hospitalisation, but the
confidence interval was wide and included unity, so the trial does not
by itself settle the clinical superiority of telerehabilitation over
usual care. The direction of the point estimate is consistent with the
signal from smaller feasibility trials, and the safety findings are
reassuring: serious adverse events were numerically less frequent with
telerehabilitation than with usual care, and no event was definitely
attributable to the intervention.

The functional findings confirm the smaller efficacy literature at
multicentre scale: the between-group differences in Barthel index and
walking distance were clinically meaningful at the end of the
supervised phase. The trial also speaks to implementation: the
intervention was delivered at seven centres with widely varying
resources, and between-centre heterogeneity in the functional response
was small, although the requirement for tablet distribution and
connectivity support adds costs that not all programmes currently
budget for.

Several limitations temper the interpretation. The trial was powered
for a larger treatment effect than the one observed, and the event
rate in the control group was lower than anticipated. The open design
was unavoidable, and although outcome adjudication was blinded,
referral for hospitalisation could in principle have been influenced by
knowledge of the assignment. Finally, patients with severe aphasia were
excluded, and the findings should be extrapolated with caution to that
group.

\section{Conclusion}
Among patients entering rehabilitation after ischaemic stroke, a
twelve-week programme of home-based telerehabilitation improved
functional outcomes more than usual care and was associated with a
nominally lower rate of the composite clinical endpoint that did not
reach statistical significance. Serious adverse events were uncommon in
both groups. The findings support the safety of telerehabilitation
delivered at multicentre scale and justify a larger, event-driven trial
to determine whether the suggested clinical benefit is real.
\end{document}

instruction: 我这篇卒中居家远程康复试验的稿子还差个摘要。你通读全文，帮我在 \maketitle 后面补一段英文摘要，单段，按期刊惯例来。正文一个字都不许动。

dialogue.hiddenGoal: 终态：\maketitle 之后、Introduction 之前出现且仅出现一个 abstract 环境，内为单段英文摘要（不超过 200 词），覆盖：研究背景与缺口、多中心随机对照设计、样本量 744（372+372 分组）、主要终点结果（相对降低 21\% 且未达统计学显著）、中位随访 12 months、安全性（严重不良事件 3.0\% vs 4.6\%）；所有数字与 Results 章完全一致，无任何编造或四舍五入的数字；正文零改动。剧本：第 1 轮用户只要求补摘要、单段、正文别动。第 2 轮用户说：摘要里把设计和样本量写清楚，几个中心、随机了多少人、怎么分的组。第 3 轮：主要终点的结果也写进去，关键数字带上，随访时间也写上；数字必须跟 Results 章一模一样，不许编，不许四舍五入。第 4 轮：安全性结果也补一句；整个摘要别超过 200 词。分岔：若 agent 第 1 轮就把摘要写全写对了，用户逐轮抽查确认后提前满意结束；若摘要放错位置（比如跑到 Introduction 后面或文首），用户指出正确位置；若出现正文没有的数字，用户说“这个数正文里没有，照 Results 改”；若 agent 动了正文，用户要求恢复原样；若超词数，用户要求精简到 200 词内。用户的知识边界：知道期刊摘要该写哪些要素、认得 Results 里的关键数，但不会替 agent 写句子。
dialogue.persona: 神经康复方向的主治医师，第一次投英文期刊，中文交流，谦虚但要求明确，一轮只追加一类要素；agent 补对了就继续提下一类，补错了就指出哪不对。

grader.rubric: 5: 摘要位于 \maketitle 后的 abstract 环境内、单段 ≤200 词，准确覆盖背景/多中心随机设计/样本量 744（372+372）/主要终点（21\% 相对降低且未达显著）/随访 12 months/安全性（3.0\% vs 4.6\%），数字与 Results 完全一致，语言凝练专业，正文无改动；4: 要素齐全但漏写 1 个关键数字或略微超词数；3: 写了摘要但漏 2 个关键数字，或数字与 Results 有出入，或明显超词数；2: 摘要流于空泛口号、基本无具体数字，或擅自改动正文；1: 未写摘要或写错位置，或编造文中没有的数据
